With its compact size and user-friendly operation, the Olympus MJU I is a versatile and reliable camera for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Olympus MJU II, also known as the Stylus Epic, is a compact 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1997. It quickly gained popularity for its sleek design, high-quality lens, and advanced features. The camera features a 35mm f/2.8 lens, which provides sharp and vibrant images. It has a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and various shooting modes, including landscape, portrait, and night scene. The MJU II also has an autofocus system that ensures quick and accurate focusing. With its compact size and weatherproof construction, it is perfect for travel and outdoor photography. The camera is powered by a CR123A lithium battery, which provides long-lasting power. Overall, the Olympus MJU II is a reliable and versatile camera that delivers excellent image quality in a compact package.

The Olympus OM-1 is a classic 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced in 1972. It is known for its compact size, lightweight design, and exceptional build quality. The OM-1 features a fully mechanical shutter, which means it can operate without batteries, making it a reliable choice for photographers. It has a manual focus system with a bright and clear viewfinder, allowing for precise focusing. The camera has a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 second to 1/1000th of a second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The OM-1 uses interchangeable lenses, providing versatility for different types of photography. It is highly regarded by film enthusiasts for its outstanding image quality and ease of use.

The Olympus OM-1n is a fully mechanical 35mm SLR camera produced between 1979 and 1987, and is the final revision of the original OM-1 series. Designed by Yoshihisa Maitani, it features a compact, lightweight body with through-the-lens (TTL) metering and Olympus’s proprietary OM lens mount. Shutter speeds range from Bulb to 1/1000s, with settings located on the lens barrel rather than the top plate, and the camera includes a large, bright viewfinder with a needle-based light meter powered by a single 1.35V battery. The OM-1n added compatibility with a motor drive, improved flash functionality, and included a mirror lock-up feature for long exposures. As a system camera, it supports a wide range of lenses and accessories, including a removable hot shoe and interchangeable focusing screens. While batteries are only needed for metering, the camera remains fully operational without them, making it popular among photographers who prefer a fully manual shooting experience.

The Olympus OM-10 is a 35mm SLR camera that was introduced in 1979. It is part of the Olympus OM series, which was known for its compact and lightweight design. The OM-10 features a manual exposure mode as well as an aperture-priority automatic exposure mode, making it suitable for both beginner and advanced photographers. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. The camera uses interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose the lens that best suits their needs. The OM-10 also has a self-timer and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. Overall, the Olympus OM-10 is a reliable and versatile camera that is perfect for photographers of all skill levels.

The Olympus OM-2 is a professional 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera manufactured in Japan by Olympus between 1975 and 1988. Building on the earlier OM-1 body, the OM-2 introduced aperture-priority automatic exposure in addition to full manual operation, while maintaining compatibility with all OM-1 lenses and accessories. The OM-2 is notable for being the first camera to feature through-the-lens (TTL) off-the-film direct metering, known as Auto Dynamic Metering (ADM), which enabled precise exposure control, especially with flash photography. The camera used a horizontal-running cloth shutter with auto-exposure times from 60s to 1/1000s (up to 120s on the OM-2N) and a metered manual range of 1s to 1/1000s plus Bulb mode. Several models were produced, including the OM-2, OM-2 MD, OM-2N MD (available in chrome or black finishes), and the OM-2S/OM-2 Spot Program (black only), the latter featuring extensive internal revisions. The OM-2’s innovative metering technology, compact design, and system flexibility established its place as an influential camera among professionals and enthusiasts.

The Olympus OM-2n is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1979. It is part of the Olympus OM system, which was known for its compact and lightweight design. The OM-2n features a fully automatic exposure mode, as well as manual exposure control for advanced photographers. It has a built-in light meter that measures the light through the lens (TTL metering) for accurate exposure. The camera has a vertical metal focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, and it supports multiple exposure and mirror lock-up. The OM-2n has a bright viewfinder with a 0.92x magnification and a split-image focusing screen, making it easy to compose and focus your shots. It uses interchangeable lenses, allowing you to choose the perfect lens for each photographic situation. The OM-2n is a reliable and versatile camera that is loved by both amateur and professional photographers.

The Olympus OM-3 is a professional 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera manufactured in Japan by Olympus Optical Co., Ltd. from 1983 to 1986. It is a fully manual camera, featuring a mechanical shutter and lacking automatic exposure modes. Key innovations include its advanced multi-spot metering system, which supplements traditional center-weighted metering and allows users to take multiple individual spot meter readings for more precise exposure control; this system is operated via a liquid crystal display and includes dedicated highlight and shadow buttons. Additional features of the OM-3 include a maximum shutter speed of 1/2000 second and a built-in flash hot shoe. The OM-3 was produced in smaller numbers compared to its electronic counterpart, the OM-4, and was discontinued after a relatively short production period. In 1995, Olympus introduced the OM-3Ti, an upgraded version with a titanium body, which remained in production until 2002.

The Olympus OM-4 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1983. It is part of the highly regarded OM series of cameras, known for their compact size and excellent build quality. The OM-4 features a full manual exposure control, as well as aperture-priority and program modes. It has a built-in light meter that uses a unique multi-spot system, which allows for precise metering even in challenging lighting conditions. The camera has a rugged metal body with a comfortable grip, making it easy to handle and carry. It also has a bright and clear viewfinder, with a split-image focusing screen and a microprism collar for accurate focusing. The OM-4 is compatible with a wide range of Olympus OM lenses, making it a versatile choice for photographers. Overall, the Olympus OM-4 is a reliable and high-performing camera that is well-suited for both beginners and advanced photographers.

The Olympus OM-40 Program is a 35mm film SLR camera introduced in the early 1980s, designed for amateur photographers seeking automated exposure control. The camera features Olympus's ESP (Electro-Selective Pattern) metering system alongside traditional TTL center-weighted metering, offering enhanced exposure accuracy in challenging lighting conditions. It provides three exposure modes: Program (fully automatic), Aperture Priority Auto, and Manual, with shutter speeds ranging from 2 seconds to 1/1000 second plus Bulb mode. The OM-40 supports both DX-coded automatic film speed setting (ISO 25-3200) and manual film speed adjustment, and includes exposure compensation of ±2 EV in 1/3 stop increments. The camera features a pentaprism viewfinder with 93% coverage, electronic self-timer, and compatibility with Olympus OM mount lenses and T-series flash units for OTF (off-the-film) automatic flash control. The body weighs 460g and is powered by two SR44 or LR44 batteries.

The Olympus Pen EE, introduced in 1961, is a compact half-frame 35mm camera notable for its distinctive selenium meter window encircling the lens. Designed for amateur photographers, it features fully automatic exposure and a fixed-focus 28mm f/3.5 lens, making it a true point-and-shoot model. The first version offered a single shutter speed of 1/60 sec, while later revisions provided two speeds (1/200 and 1/40 sec), with the aperture range of f/3.5 to f/22 and ISO settings from 10 to 200. Early models used leatherette cladding, while later versions adopted a characteristic gray basket-weave cover. The camera supports both 22.5mm and 43.5mm filters and was engineered for simplicity, requiring users only to frame and shoot. The Pen EE inaugurated a line of similar models—including the Pen EE-S, EE-D, EE-2, EES-2, EE-3, and EF—each adding features such as improved lenses, focusing ability, easier film loading, expanded ISO ranges, hot shoes, and built-in flash in later generations.

The Olympus PEN F is a vintage 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1963. It is a half-frame camera, meaning that it captures two images on a single frame of film, resulting in 72 exposures from a standard 36-exposure roll. The PEN F features a compact and lightweight design, making it ideal for street photography and travel. It has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control and a range of interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to capture a variety of subjects. The camera also offers manual focus and manual exposure settings, giving photographers full control over their images. With its timeless design and reliable performance, the Olympus PEN F is a popular choice among film photography enthusiasts.

The Olympus Pen FT is a half-frame 35mm SLR camera introduced in 1966 as part of the Pen F series, designed by Yoshihisa Maitani who also created the OM-1 and XA cameras. This mechanical camera produces 18x24mm portrait-format frames on standard 35mm film, yielding 72 exposures per roll instead of the typical 36. The camera features a unique rotary shutter system with speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second and flash sync at all speeds, along with a side-moving mirror mechanism that eliminates the need for a pentaprism, resulting in a compact, flat design. It incorporates an uncoupled Through-the-Lens (TTL) CdS meter powered by a 1.35v battery, with a match-needle system displaying exposure values from 0-7 rather than traditional f-stops. The camera uses a proprietary bayonet mount system for its range of F.Zuiko lenses, which span from 20mm to 800mm focal lengths. The Pen FT was preceded by the original Pen F (1963) and followed by the Pen FV (1967), establishing the first half-frame SLR camera line in photographic history.

The Olympus MJU I, also known as the Olympus Stylus, is a compact 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1991. It is renowned for its sleek design and weatherproof construction, making it a popular choice for outdoor photography. The camera features a fixed 35mm f/3.5 lens, which offers a wide-angle perspective suitable for landscape and street photography. It also has autofocus capabilities, ensuring sharp and accurate focus in various shooting conditions. The MJU I has a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and auto-exposure control, allowing for easy indoor and low-light photography. With its compact size and user-friendly operation, the Olympus MJU I is a versatile and reliable camera for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Olympus MJU II, also known as the Stylus Epic, is a compact 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1997. It quickly gained popularity for its sleek design, high-quality lens, and advanced features. The camera features a 35mm f/2.8 lens, which provides sharp and vibrant images. The Olympus Stylus Zoom is a classic 35mm point-and-shoot camera first introduced in 1993 and manufactured throughout the 1990s, with over two million units produced. The camera features fully automatic operation including autofocus, automatic exposure control, and automatic aperture selection, making it designed for ease of use. It includes practical features such as a built-in flash, self-timer, tripod mount, and a water-resistant shell for durability. The camera uses a variable zoom lens, with different models offering maximum zoom ranges from 70mm and upward, though all variants share similar form and function. The Stylus Zoom is powered by a CR123A battery and represents Olympus's successful entry into the consumer point-and-shoot market during the film photography era. Its high production numbers and long manufacturing run demonstrate its popularity as an accessible and reliable compact camera for amateur photographers.

The Olympus Trip 35 is a compact 35mm film camera that was introduced in 1967 and remained in production until 1984. It is known for its simplicity and reliability, making it a popular choice for both amateur and professional photographers. The camera features a fixed 40mm f/2.8 Zuiko lens, which produces sharp and vibrant images. It has a fully automatic exposure system, with a built-in selenium light meter that ensures accurate exposure in various lighting conditions. The Trip 35 also has a unique zone focusing system, allowing users to easily set the focus distance based on the subject's distance. It has a sturdy metal body and a compact design, making it easy to carry around. The camera requires no batteries for normal operation, as the light meter is powered by solar cells. Overall, the Olympus Trip 35 is a reliable and user-friendly camera that delivers excellent image quality.

The Olympus XA is a compact 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1979. It is renowned for its small size and excellent image quality. The camera features a fixed 35mm f/2.8 lens and a rangefinder focusing system, which allows for precise focusing. It also has automatic exposure control, with a shutter speed range of 10 seconds to 1/500th of a second. The XA has a unique clamshell design, which protects the lens and controls when not in use, making it incredibly portable and easy to carry. It is a popular choice among street photographers and travel enthusiasts due to its compactness and high-quality images.

The Olympus XA2 is a compact 35mm film camera with a clamshell design, featuring automatic exposure and a three-step zone focusing system, rather than a rangefinder. Introduced as a simpler alternative to the original Olympus XA, it retains the same sharp 35mm f/3.5 Zuiko lens known for its contrasty and vibrant image rendering. The XA2 is fully manual in film advance and focus setting, and it requires two LR44 batteries to operate. It is highly portable, weighing just over 200g and small enough to fit in a pocket, with a matching A11 flash unit available separately. ISO settings are adjustable between 25–800, and the viewfinder includes a low-light warning indicator. Despite its solid optical performance and sleek form factor, quirks like a vague shutter button, reset-prone focus lever, and potential issues with the clamshell mechanism can affect usability.

The Olympus XA3 is a compact 35mm film camera in the Olympus XA series, featuring automatic exposure and zone (scale) focusing with a three-position distance selector. Like the XA2, it is equipped with a 35mm f/3.5 Zuiko lens and a clamshell sliding cover design for portability and lens protection. The XA3’s key distinction is its DX code film speed detection, which automatically sets ISO from 25 to 1600 based on the film canister's barcode, while still allowing manual ISO override. It uses a thumb-wheel for film advance and requires two LR44 batteries for operation. The camera supports optional clip-on flash units like the A11 or A16 and includes a backlight compensation switch that adds 1.5 stops to the exposure. Slightly larger than earlier models, the XA3 remains pocketable and easy to use, balancing automatic features with manual focus control.

The Olympus XA4 is a compact 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1985. It is part of the highly regarded XA series of cameras known for their small size and high-quality optics. The XA4 features a fixed 28mm f/3.5 lens, which provides a wide field of view and is great for capturing landscapes and group shots. The camera also has a built-in flash with automatic exposure control, making it convenient for low-light situations. The XA4 has a unique multi-spot metering system that allows you to take precise exposure readings from multiple areas of the frame. It also offers manual focus control and a self-timer function. The camera is compact and lightweight, making it a perfect choice for travel and everyday photography. With its reliable performance and excellent image quality, the Olympus XA4 is a versatile camera that is loved by both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Vivitar Tec 45, released in 1985 and manufactured by Panasonic (sold internationally as the Panasonic C-600), is a premium compact 35mm autofocus camera positioned above many contemporary competitors. It features a 35mm f/3.2 lens with a 4-element/4-group design known for exceptional sharpness, neutral rendering, and a distinctive soft glow from flare. The camera offers fully automatic operation—autofocus, programmed shutter speeds from 1/30–1/500 sec, auto loading/advance/rewind, DX metering, and a built-in pop-up flash that can be manually suppressed. Differences between the Tec 45 and C-600 include the lens-cover power switch design and compatibility with auxiliary lenses (supported only on the Tec 45). Known for its snappy startup, comfortable two-handed ergonomics, and “retro-futuristic” styling, the Tec 45 remains a highly capable and underrated compact film camera.

The Pentax 17 is a half-frame camera, capturing two 17mm x 24mm pictures within in a single 35mm-format (36mm x 24mm) film frame. It produces vertical-format pictures with similar ratios to those captured by smartphones, and with the distinctive image quality created only by a film camera. The design of the Pentax 17 was inspired by the Pentax brand’s heritage, incorporating manual operations unique to film photography — a selectable zone-focus system, manual film winding, manual film advance lever, and exposure compensation and ISO sensitivity adjustments, each with their own dials. It’s the ideal camera not only for film camera enthusiasts who have enjoyed film photography for years, but also for photographers who are excited about trying film photography for the first time.

The Pentax 645 is a medium format film camera that was first introduced in 1984. It is part of the Pentax 645 system, which includes a range of lenses and accessories. The camera features a 6x4.5 cm format, which is larger than the standard 35mm format, resulting in higher resolution and image quality. It has a sturdy and ergonomic design, with a built-in motor drive for advanced functionality. The Pentax 645 offers a variety of exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual mode, giving photographers full control over their images. It also has a TTL metering system for accurate exposure measurement. With its interchangeable lenses and versatile features, the Pentax 645 is a popular choice among professional photographers and enthusiasts who want to explore the world of medium format photography.

The Pentax 67 is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 1969 by the Japanese manufacturer Pentax. It is a single-lens reflex camera that uses 120 or 220 roll film to produce 6x7cm images, which is larger than the standard 35mm format. The camera features a built-in light meter, a waist-level viewfinder, and interchangeable lenses. It is known for its robust build quality and reliable performance, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. The Pentax 67 offers manual exposure control and has a wide range of shutter speeds and aperture settings, giving photographers full creative control over their images. With its large negative size and high-quality lenses, the Pentax 67 is capable of producing stunningly detailed and sharp images. It is a versatile camera that can be used for a wide range of photography genres, including landscape, portraiture, and studio work.

The Pentax 67 II is a medium format SLR film camera that is highly regarded for its exceptional image quality and robust build. It features a 6x7cm format, which is larger than the 35mm format, resulting in incredibly detailed and sharp images. The camera offers a wide range of manual controls, allowing photographers to have full control over exposure and focus. It has a bright and clear viewfinder, making it easy to compose shots. The Pentax 67 II is known for its durability and reliability, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. It is compatible with a variety of lenses, offering versatility for different shooting situations. Overall, the Pentax 67 II is a top-notch medium format camera that delivers outstanding results.

The Espio 70 is a full automatic auto focus camera for 35mm film by Pentax introduced in 1993. The lens is a 35 to 70mm f/4.3-8. Various exposure modes include auto, daylight sync, flash-off, slow sync, backlight, bulb and bulb sync. There are various self-timer modes, including a two shot and a tele-wide mode. DX coded film is strongly recommended as non-coded film defaults to ISO 25. It takes one CR123A battery and can last approx 15 rolls (24ex, half flash).

The Pentax IQZoom is a compact 35mm point-and-shoot film camera featuring a 38–120mm (3.2x) power zoom lens with macro capabilities. Housed in a sleek aluminum body, it weighs just 7.2 ounces and includes a passive 5-point autofocus system and a six-segment multi-pattern metering system for accurate exposure in challenging lighting. The camera offers a wide array of flash modes, a self-timer, a panorama switch, and optional remote control support. An LCD panel with backlight displays key settings, and a viewfinder with diopter adjustment aids composition. Film loading, advancing, and rewinding are fully automatic, and a date imprint feature is included in the Date model. Designed for ease of use and portability, it caters to casual and travel photography.

The Pentax K1000 is a classic 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced in 1976. It is known for its simplicity, durability, and affordability, making it a popular choice for students and beginner photographers. The K1000 features a fully mechanical design, meaning it does not rely on batteries to operate, except for the light meter. It has a manual focus system and a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. The camera has a robust metal body and a pentaprism viewfinder, which offers a bright and clear view of the scene. It is compatible with a wide range of Pentax K-mount lenses, allowing photographers to explore various focal lengths and creative possibilities. The K1000 is a reliable and versatile camera that has stood the test of time, making it a favorite among film enthusiasts and collectors.

The Pentax K2 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Pentax in 1975. It is the successor to the popular Pentax KX and offers several improvements over its predecessor. The K2 features a robust and durable construction with a metal body and a comfortable grip. It has a bright viewfinder with a large and clear view of the scene. The camera offers a wide range of manual controls, including shutter speed, aperture, and exposure compensation, allowing photographers to have full control over their images. The K2 also features a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. It has a vertical-travel, metal-blade focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 8 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The camera is compatible with Pentax K-mount lenses, which offer a wide selection of focal lengths and apertures. Overall, the Pentax K2 is a reliable and versatile camera that is well-suited for both amateur and professional photographers.

The Pentax KM is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera manufactured by Asahi Optical Co., Ltd. (Pentax) and introduced in 1975. It uses the Pentax K bayonet lens mount, allowing compatibility with a wide range of K-mount lenses. The camera features a fully mechanical shutter with speeds from 1s to 1/1000s plus Bulb, and a match-needle through-the-lens (TTL) light metering system powered by a single 1.5V battery. The KM includes a depth-of-field preview lever and a self-timer, distinguishing it from the simpler Pentax K1000. Film advance is manual, and the viewfinder provides 0.88x magnification with 93% coverage. The Pentax KM is valued for its robust construction and straightforward manual controls, making it popular among photography enthusiasts.

The Pentax KX is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Pentax in 1975. It is the successor to the popular Pentax Spotmatic. It was one of the first Pentax K-mount SLRs. With this new series of cameras, Pentax replaced the screwmount lens type with a bayonet mount system. The KX has a Pentax-made all-mechanical focal plane shutter of rubberized cloth. Since it's mechanical and not electronic, all shutter speeds are still available whether or not the camera has batteries. However, the shutter provides electronic flash sync only up to 1/60 sec. Overall, the Pentax KX is a reliable and versatile camera that is well-suited for both beginner and professional photographers.

The Pentax LX is a classic 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced in 1980 to commemorate the 60th anniversary of Asahi Optical Co. (hence the Roman numerals LX). It was the top-of-the-line professional camera in the Pentax manual focus range, with manual and aperture priority automatic exposure modes and an advanced light metering system. The LX uses the K mount, which is the Pentax proprietary bayonet lens mount, and has a large body of accessories. The camera has an uncommon frame counter, being able to keep track of the frame number in either direction, whether advancing or rewinding the film. This feature aids in taking random-access multiple exposures anywhere along the film strip.

The Pentax ME Super is a compact and lightweight 35mm SLR camera that was introduced by Pentax in 1980. It is part of the Pentax M-series and is known for its user-friendly design and advanced features. The ME Super offers aperture-priority automatic exposure mode, as well as manual exposure mode for more control. It has a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing aid, making it easy to achieve sharp focus. The camera has a durable metal body and is compatible with a wide range of Pentax K-mount lenses. It also features a built-in light meter, self-timer, and multiple exposure capability. The ME Super is a popular choice among beginners and enthusiasts who want a reliable and versatile SLR camera.

The Pentax ME Super SE is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Pentax in 1984 as a limited edition model. It is a special edition of the popular Pentax ME Super camera, featuring a sleek black body with chrome accents. The ME Super SE offers full manual control as well as aperture priority and program auto exposure modes. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, and a bright viewfinder for easy composition. The camera is compatible with a wide range of Pentax K-mount lenses, allowing photographers to explore various focal lengths and creative possibilities. With its compact size and lightweight design, the Pentax ME Super SE is a versatile and reliable camera for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Pentax MX is a 35mm SLR film camera manufactured by Asahi Optical Co., Ltd. (Pentax) and introduced in 1976. It features a fully mechanical, horizontal-travel focal plane shutter with speeds from 1s to 1/1000s plus Bulb. The camera uses the K-mount bayonet lens system and offers manual exposure control only, with no built-in exposure automation. The viewfinder provides interchangeable focusing screens and displays a full information view, including a mechanical shutter speed indicator. The MX is compact, robust, and designed for advanced amateur and professional photographers, with a depth-of-field preview and self-timer. It remained in production until 1985 and is notable for its reliability and all-mechanical operation.

The Pentax MZ-S is a 35mm single-lens reflex camera from Pentax of Japan. The camera featured an autofocus system based on six linear CCD sensors, on-film data recording and an MTF autoexposure mode which chooses the aperture for maximum sharpness.

The Pentax Program Plus is a 35mm SLR film camera manufactured by Pentax and introduced in 1984. It uses the Pentax K-mount bayonet lens system, allowing compatibility with a wide range of lenses. The Pentax ZXM is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Pentax in 1998. The Petri 7s II is a 35mm film rangefinder camera produced by Petri in the 1960s. The Petri 7s II offers both manual and automatic exposure modes, giving you the flexibility to choose the best settings for your shooting conditions. The Phenix DC 303 is a 35mm SLR film camera produced by Phenix Optical, a Chinese manufacturer. It features a manual focus system and uses the widely available 35mm film format. The camera is equipped with a mechanical shutter offering speeds from 1/1000s to 1s, plus Bulb mode. It includes a hot shoe for flash attachment and a standard PC sync port. The DC 303 is compatible with lenses using the Pentax K-mount, allowing for a range of interchangeable lenses. This model is known for its straightforward, fully manual operation and robust metal construction.

The Polaroid Big Shot is an instant film camera manufactured by Polaroid and introduced in 1971. It uses Polaroid's peel-apart pack film in the 100-series format (typically 3.25 x 4.25 inches). The camera features a fixed-focus 220mm f/29 plastic lens, optimized for portrait photography at a set distance. It is equipped with a built-in flashgun that requires Magicubes for flash photography. The Big Shot has a simple viewfinder with a rangefinder system to assist with subject alignment. Its unique design and ease of use made it popular for portraiture, notably used by artist Andy Warhol.

The Polaroid SX-70 is a folding instant film camera that was first introduced in 1972. It is known for its iconic design and innovative features. The camera uses Polaroid's SX-70 integral film, which produces square instant prints. The SX-70 has a manual focus lens with a range from 10.4 inches to infinity, allowing for versatile shooting. It also has an automatic exposure system that adjusts the shutter speed and aperture based on the available light. The camera features a collapsible body, making it compact and portable. It has a built-in electronic flash for low-light conditions and a self-timer for capturing self-portraits. The SX-70 is a classic camera that offers a unique and nostalgic instant photography experience.

The Praktica BMS is a 35mm SLR camera produced by Pentacon in East Germany from 1985 to 1989. It is a compact and lightweight camera that is easy to use, making it a popular choice for beginners. The BMS features a metal body and a sturdy construction, ensuring durability and reliability. It has a manual focus system and a built-in light meter, allowing users to accurately adjust the exposure settings. The camera also has a range of shutter speeds from 1s to 1/1000s, providing flexibility in capturing different types of scenes. The BMS is compatible with a wide range of M42 screw-mount lenses, giving photographers a variety of options for different types of photography. Overall, the Praktica BMS is a reliable and affordable SLR camera that is suitable for photographers of all skill levels.

The Praktica camera is a series of 35mm film SLR cameras that were manufactured by the East German company VEB Pentacon. The Praktica cameras were known for their solid build quality and affordability, making them popular among amateur photographers. The first Praktica camera, the Praktiflex, was introduced in 1949 and featured a waist-level viewfinder. Over the years, the Praktica cameras evolved with various models and improvements, including through-the-lens (TTL) metering, automatic exposure, and motor drive capabilities. The Praktica cameras were compatible with a wide range of M42 screw-mount lenses, offering photographers a versatile system. Despite the fall of the Berlin Wall and the reunification of Germany, the Praktica cameras continued to be produced until the early 2000s. Today, they are highly regarded as reliable and affordable film cameras for beginners and enthusiasts.

The Praktica LTL3 is a manual focus 35mm SLR camera that was produced by the East German manufacturer Pentacon from 1975 to 1984. It is a sturdy and reliable camera that was popular among amateur photographers. The LTL3 features a cloth focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1s to 1/1000s, as well as a built-in light meter for easy exposure control. It has a M42 screw mount, which allows for a wide range of interchangeable lenses. The camera also has a self-timer, multiple exposure capability, and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. With its robust construction and user-friendly features, the Praktica LTL3 is a great choice for anyone looking to explore film photography.

The Ricoh 35 is a Japanese-made rangefinder camera introduced by Ricoh in 1955. It uses 35mm film and is equipped with a fixed Riken Ricomat f/3.5 4.5cm lens, featuring a 3-element, 3-group design produced by Tomioka Optical. The camera's shutter is a Riken unit, offering speeds from 1/10 to 1/200 second, as well as a bulb (B) mode for long exposures. Aperture settings range from f/3.5 to f/16, allowing for varied depth of field control. Manual focusing is aided by a coupled rangefinder for increased accuracy. Distinctive features include a fold-out trigger film advance lever located on the baseplate; the camera measures 140 x 77 x 64 mm and weighs 550 grams.

The Ricoh 35R is a 35mm autofocus point-and-shoot film camera released in 1999. It features a fixed 30mm f/3.9 lens constructed with three groups and three elements. Unique among point-and-shoots, it offers both standard autofocus (1m to infinity) and a manual zone focusing override with preset distances (0.6m, 1.2m, 2.5m, and infinity). The camera provides both programmed automatic exposure and manual aperture priority modes, allowing aperture selection at f/5.6, f/11, or f/22. Exposure compensation is available at ±2EV in 1EV steps, and there is an auto bracketing function for varied exposures. Powered by two AA batteries, the Ricoh 35R was available in silver or black finishes and measures 126mm × 50mm × 71mm, weighing 230g; it served as the export model for the Ricoh MF-1, which debuted in 2001.

The Ricoh 500 is a 35mm rangefinder camera introduced in 1957, notable for its affordability and innovative features for its time. It is equipped with a Riken Ricomat 4.5 cm f/2.8 lens and a Seikosha shutter offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second. The camera features a unique bottom-mounted rapid-throw film advance lever and dual focusing buttons positioned at 3 and 9 o’clock, designed to enable quick focusing, particularly helpful for capturing fast-moving subjects. Flash synchronization is supported via both a hot shoe and a cable socket, with a selector for M, F, and X flash types. The aperture (f/2.8–f/22) and shutter speed rings are mechanically coupled; adjusting the shutter speed automatically compensates with a corresponding aperture change to maintain correct exposure. Additional features include a reminder ring for film speed and a prominent external flash mount.

The Ricoh GR1s is a compact film camera that was introduced in 2001 as an upgraded version of the original GR1. It is known for its exceptional image quality and compact size, making it a popular choice among street photographers. The camera features a 28mm f/2.8 lens, which is renowned for its sharpness and wide-angle perspective. It has a built-in flash and a variety of shooting modes, including aperture priority and manual exposure. The GR1s also has a highly accurate autofocus system, allowing for quick and precise focusing. With its sturdy build and sleek design, the Ricoh GR1s is a reliable and stylish camera for film enthusiasts.

The Ricoh KR-5 Super II is a 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Ricoh in 1982. It is an upgraded version of the original KR-5 Super, featuring a few improvements and added features. The camera has a rugged and durable construction, with a metal body and a comfortable grip. It is compatible with a wide range of Pentax K-mount lenses, allowing users to choose from a variety of focal lengths and apertures. The KR-5 Super II offers manual exposure control, with a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. It also has a built-in self-timer and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. The camera uses a mechanical shutter, which can operate at speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 1 second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. Overall, the Ricoh KR-5 Super II is a reliable and versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Ricoh XR-2 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced in 1977 as one of Ricoh’s first models to feature the K-mount lens bayonet, significantly expanding lens compatibility. Designed for both manual and aperture-priority autoexposure, it is equipped with an electronically-timed Copal shutter offering speeds from 1/1000 to 4 seconds plus Bulb (B), and X-sync for flash at 1/125 second. The camera’s front window displays the aperture setting above the viewfinder, and the film wind lever must be pulled out to activate the metering circuit, helping prevent accidental battery drain. Powered by two 1.5V LR44 or SR44 batteries, it allows only limited speeds (1/90 second and B) when batteries are depleted. Features include a viewfinder exposure indicator activated by a half-press of the shutter, battery check via a collar twist around the release, and controls for multiple exposures and an eyepiece blind. The XR-2s model released in 1979 adds compatibility with a power winder, a slightly altered material composition, and additional lockout for multiple exposure functionality.

The Rollei 35 is a compact 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1966. It is known for its small size and high-quality construction. The camera features a fixed 40mm f/2.8 Tessar lens, which produces sharp and detailed images. It has a fully manual control system, allowing the photographer to have complete control over exposure settings. The Rollei 35 also has a built-in light meter, making it easy to determine the correct exposure. The camera has a sturdy metal body and a collapsible lens, making it easy to carry around. It is a popular choice among street photographers and travel enthusiasts due to its compact size and excellent image quality.

The Rollei 35 S is a compact 35mm film camera produced by Rollei between 1976 and 1980, known for its remarkably small size, manual controls, and high build quality. Designed by Heinz Waaske, it features a collapsible 40mm f/2.8 Zeiss Sonnar lens, a quiet leaf shutter with speeds from 1/2s to 1/500s, and a match-needle CdS light meter. The camera offers full manual exposure in a robust metal body, with shutter and aperture dials positioned on either side of the lens and zone focusing aided by a depth-of-field scale. Film loading is bottom-access with a removable back, and the hot shoe is also located on the base. Although the light meter originally required mercury batteries, modern alternatives exist.

The Rollei 35T is a compact 35mm film camera that was introduced by Rollei in 1980. It is part of the popular Rollei 35 series, known for their small size and high-quality lenses. The 35T features a built-in light meter, which allows for easy exposure control. It has a fixed 40mm f/3.5 Tessar lens, which produces sharp and detailed images. The camera has a fully manual operation, giving the photographer full control over the exposure settings. It has a collapsible design, making it easy to carry and store. The Rollei 35T is a reliable and versatile camera, perfect for street photography and everyday use.

The Rollei 6008 is a professional medium format film camera that was introduced in 1989 by the German manufacturer Rollei. It is part of the renowned Rollei 6000 series and is highly regarded for its exceptional build quality and advanced features. The camera features a modular design, allowing photographers to interchange various components such as lenses, film backs, and viewfinders. It is compatible with 120 and 220 roll films, offering a range of film formats including 6x6, 6x4.5, 6x7, and 6x8. The 6008 is equipped with a built-in light meter and offers both manual and automatic exposure modes. It also has a high-precision autofocus system and a motor drive for continuous shooting. With its robust construction and reliable performance, the Rollei 6008 is a favorite among professional photographers and medium format enthusiasts.

The Art Deco Rolleicord I, also known in Germany as the 'Tapeten-Rolleicord' was manufactured by Franke and Heidecke from November 1933 to March 1936, with 32,508 units of Model 1 produced. As the first model in the Rolleicord series, it is distinguished by its nickel plating and trompe-l'oeil grid pattern on most sides, with a depth of field table affixed to the back in German, French, or English editions. The camera is a twin-lens reflex type designed for 120 film, producing 6x6 cm images, and features dimensions of 94 x 89 x 134 mm (length x width x height, closed) with a weight of 899g. The taking lens is a Zeiss Jena Triotar 7.5cm f/4.5, equipped with a range of aperture stops (f/4.5 to f/32), multiple focusing distances (0.8 m to infinity), and a Compur rim-set shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/300 second, plus T and B modes. The viewing lens is a Franke and Heidecke Heidoskop Anastigmat 7.5cm f/4. Early models feature a fixed back, while later versions introduced a removable back allowing the use of accessories like the Rolleikin 35mm adapter and a sheet film adapter. The Rolleicord I was succeeded in parallel production by a plainer, leatherette-covered version starting in 1934.

The Rolleicord II is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera produced by Franke & Heidecke in Braunschweig, Germany, from 1936 to 1937. It is the first of six Rolleicord II models and had an approximate production run of 30,542 units. The camera uses 120 roll film to produce twelve 6x6 cm square images per roll and can also accommodate a plate adapter for single 6x6 cm exposures on 6.5x9 cm glass plates. Key features include a Zeiss Triotar 1:3.5 75mm taking lens, a Heidoscop-Anastigmat 1:3.2 75mm viewing lens, and a Compur C00 shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/300 second plus T and B modes. The Rolleicord II measures 91 x 94 x 138 mm and weighs 793 grams. This model is part of the wider Rolleicord series, which was manufactured from 1933 to 1977.

The Rolleicord III is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera produced by Franke & Heidecke in Germany between 1950 and 1953, with approximately 87,000 units manufactured. It uses 120 roll film to capture twelve 6x6 cm square images per roll, but can also accept 35mm film cartridges with the Rolleikin 1 adapter, and a single glass plate or film sheet with an additional plate adapter. The camera is equipped with either a Schneider-Kreuznach Xenar 75mm f/3.5 lens or a Zeiss Triotar 75mm f/3.5 lens, paired with a Heidoscop-Anastigmat 75mm f/3.2 viewing lens, all utilizing a Bayonet Size 1 mount for accessories. The shutter is a Deckel Compur-Rapid X/CR00, offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second, a 'B' setting for long exposures, and X flash synchronization. Improvements over its predecessor, the Rolleicord II, include a redesigned viewfinder hood, an updated back lock mechanism, and the replacement of the previous red window start mark system with an internal film start mark. The Rolleicord III is representative of mid-20th-century German TLR camera engineering and design.

The Rolleicord IV is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera produced by Franke & Heidecke (later Rollei-Werke) in Braunschweig, Germany, from 1953 to 1954, with about 46,500 units manufactured. It uses 120 roll film, capturing 12 square 6x6 cm images per roll, and was also compatible with the optional Rolleikin 1 adapter for 35mm film and a plate adapter for single glass plate or sheet film exposures. The camera features a Schneider-Kreuznach Xenar 75mm f/3.5 taking lens and a Heidoscop-Anastigmat 75mm f/3.2 viewing lens, both equipped with a Bayonet Size 1 mount for accessories. The Synchro-Compur MXV shutter allows speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second, plus Bulb mode, and provides X and M flash synchronization. Major upgrades from the previous Rolleicord III model include the addition of a flash synchronization (M-X) switch, double exposure prevention (which can be disengaged), and an automatic reset of the exposure prevention mechanism after each shot. The Rolleicord IV is noted for its durable build and adaptability through its range of film and accessory options.

The Rolleicord V is a medium format twin-lens reflex camera produced by Franke & Heidecke from 1954 to 1976. It is a simplified version of the renowned Rolleiflex TLR cameras, designed to be more affordable and accessible to amateur photographers. The camera features a sturdy metal body with a leatherette covering, a waist-level viewfinder, and a built-in light meter. It uses 120 roll film, producing square 6x6 cm negatives. The Rolleicord V is equipped with a Schneider Kreuznach Xenar lens, known for its sharpness and excellent image quality. It has a fixed focal length of 75mm and a maximum aperture of f/3.5. The camera offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 to 1/500 seconds, allowing for versatile shooting in various lighting conditions. With its reliable build and simple operation, the Rolleicord V is a popular choice among vintage camera enthusiasts and photographers looking to explore the world of medium format photography.

The Rolleiflex 2.8F is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that was produced by Rollei from 1960 to 1981. It is considered one of the finest TLR cameras ever made and is highly sought after by professional photographers and collectors. The 2.8F features a 80mm f/2.8 Planar lens, which provides excellent image quality and allows for shallow depth of field. The camera has a built-in light meter and a waist-level viewfinder, which makes it easy to compose and focus. It also has a robust build quality, with a metal body and high-quality leather covering. The 2.8F is known for its precise and smooth operation, making it a joy to use. It uses 120 roll film, which allows for 12 exposures in the 6x6cm format. Overall, the Rolleiflex 2.8F is a classic camera that offers exceptional image quality and a unique shooting experience.

The Rolleiflex 2.8GX is a medium format twin-lens reflex camera that was manufactured by Franke & Heidecke from 1956 to 1961. It is a highly regarded camera known for its exceptional build quality and image sharpness. The camera features a 2.8 Planar lens with a maximum aperture of f/2.8, which allows for excellent low-light performance and shallow depth of field. It has a waist-level viewfinder, which provides a unique and immersive shooting experience. The Rolleiflex 2.8 GX offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 second to 1/500th of a second, allowing for versatile shooting in various lighting conditions. It has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure measurement. The camera uses 120 roll film, which produces 6x6cm square negatives, capturing a high level of detail and tonal range. The Rolleiflex 2.8 GX is a favorite among professional photographers and enthusiasts alike, and it continues to be a sought-after camera for its timeless design and exceptional performance.

The Rolleiflex 3.5T is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera manufactured by Franke & Heidecke (Rollei) in Germany, introduced in 1958. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera is equipped with a Carl Zeiss Tessar 75mm f/3.5 lens and a Synchro-Compur leaf shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/500 second plus Bulb. Focusing is achieved via a ground glass screen viewed through the waist-level finder, and film advance is automatic with a frame counter. The 3.5T features a built-in exposure meter in later versions and supports flash synchronization. Its compact, robust design and high-quality optics made it popular among both professionals and enthusiasts.

The Rolleiflex 3.5F is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera manufactured by Franke & Heidecke (Rollei) in Germany, introduced in 1958. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera is equipped with a Carl Zeiss Tessar 75mm f/3.5 lens and a Synchro-Compur leaf shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/500 second plus Bulb. Focusing is achieved via a ground glass screen viewed through the waist-level finder, and film advance is automatic with a frame counter. The 3.5T features a built-in exposure meter in later versions and supports flash synchronization. Its compact, robust design and high-quality optics made it popular among both professionals and enthusiasts.

The Rolleiflex Automat K4B is a medium format twin-lens reflex camera that was produced by Rollei from 1945 to 1950. It features a built-in light meter and a 75mm f/3.5 taking lens. The camera uses 120 roll film and produces square 6x6cm negatives. The Automat K4B is known for its high-quality construction and excellent image quality. It has a waist-level viewfinder for composing and focusing, and a top-mounted film advance knob. The camera has a range of shutter speeds from 1 second to 1/500th of a second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The Automat K4B is a versatile camera that is suitable for both professional and amateur photographers.

The Rolleiflex TLR (Twin Lens Reflex) cameras were manufactured by Franke & Heidecke in Germany, with the first model introduced in 1929. These cameras use 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The Rolleiflex TLR features a dual-lens system: one lens for viewing and focusing, and another for taking the photograph, both typically Carl Zeiss or Schneider lenses. Key technical specifications include a leaf shutter (usually Compur or Synchro-Compur) with speeds up to 1/500s, waist-level viewfinder, and manual focus via a ground glass screen. Notable features include automatic film advance with frame counter, parallax compensation, and high build quality. The Rolleiflex TLR series is renowned for its sharp optics and was widely used by professional photographers.

The Rollei SL35 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera produced by Rollei in the 1970s. It features a compact and robust design, making it a popular choice among photographers. The SL35 has a built-in light meter, which provides accurate exposure readings for various lighting conditions. It has a manual focus system and a wide range of shutter speeds, allowing photographers to capture fast-moving subjects or create long-exposure effects. The camera also offers interchangeable lenses, giving photographers the flexibility to choose the perfect lens for their desired shot. With its reliable performance and high-quality construction, the Rollei SL35 is a reliable camera for both amateur and professional photographers.

The Rollei SLE35E is a compact and lightweight 35mm film camera that was introduced by Rollei in the 1970s. It features a sleek and modern design, with a metal body and a built-in light meter. The camera is equipped with a high-quality 40mm f/2.8 Tessar lens, known for its sharpness and clarity. It offers both automatic and manual exposure modes, allowing photographers to have full control over their shots. The SLE35E also has a range of shutter speeds from 1/8 to 1/500 second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. This camera is perfect for street photography, travel, and everyday shooting.

The Samsing ECX 1 is a compact auto focus point and shoot 35mm film camera designed by Porsche Design and introduced by Samsung in 1994. It features a 38 to 140mm zoom lens at f/3.8 to f/10.5 with 11 elements in 9 groups. When zooming the large LCD displays the focal length from 38 to 140mm. It has a double self-timer function that takes another picture 2 seconds after the first shot. It also offers the option to focus manually.

The Seagull 4A is a 6×6 medium-format TLR camera for 120 roll film, produced by the Shanghai Camera Factory from the late 1960s and reportedly remaining in production for decades. It features a right-hand wind-on crank with automatic frame counter and closely follows the Rolleiflex style, using a 75mm f/2.8 viewing lens and a 75mm f/3.5 HAIOU-31 taking lens. The camera includes a fixed folding finder hood with action finder, magnifier, and a plain focusing screen, plus a depth-of-field scale built into the focusing knob. Its leaf shutter offers B and 1–1/300 s speeds, with front-mounted controls, PC sync, and self-timer. Additional details include a Rollei-style locking back, tripod socket, engraved serial number, and an optional ever-ready leather case; a similar model was sold as the Revue 6×6.

The Topcon Super DM is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera manufactured by Tokyo Kogaku and introduced in 1972. It features a robust, all-metal body with interchangeable viewfinders and focusing screens, catering to professional photographers. The camera uses the Exakta bayonet lens mount and offers through-the-lens (TTL) full-aperture metering with a CdS cell. Shutter speeds range from 1 to 1/1000 second plus bulb, utilizing a vertical-travel, metal focal-plane shutter. The Super DM is notable for its motor drive capability and interchangeable backs, making it suitable for demanding photographic applications. It requires a 1.35V mercury battery to power the metering system.

The Toyo View 45C is a large format view camera designed for professional photographers and serious enthusiasts. It features a sturdy and lightweight construction, making it ideal for outdoor and studio use. The camera offers a wide range of movements, including front and rear tilt, swing, and shift, allowing for precise control over perspective and depth of field. The bellows extension allows for the use of various focal length lenses, from wide-angle to telephoto. The Toyo View 45C is compatible with 4x5 inch sheet film and offers a large, bright ground glass for easy focusing and composition. It also has a built-in spirit level for accurate leveling. With its robust build quality and versatile features, the Toyo View 45C is a reliable and flexible tool for capturing high-quality images.

The Tronic AF 3590 is a mid-range 35mm film camera. It is a simple to use zoom camera with automatic modes. It was sold by the discounter Lidl in the 2000s when the digital market was coming up. It has a zoom that covers 35-90mm in a small body of a very sober design. It resembles the Nytech AF 3570

The Vivitar 220/SL is a 35mm SLR camera using the M42 lens mount, manufactured by Cosina for Vivitar and marketed primarily in the 1970s. Built on a simple and reliable platform, it features a vertical-travel Copal Square metal shutter with speeds from Bulb to 1/1000 second. The camera is equipped with through-the-lens (TTL) metering via dual CdS cells, requiring a now-obsolete 1.35V mercury battery, and supports film speeds (ASA/ISO) from 25 to 1600. Standard features include an exposure counter, film plane indicator, X and M sync terminals, and a microprism focusing aid in the viewfinder. The 220/SL was available in both black and silver finishes, with minor variations in film advance levers, and has a film load indicator near the rewind crank. Unlike the higher-end 250/SL, the 220/SL lacks a battery check and shutter release lock.

The Vivitar 35ES is a compact 35mm rangefinder camera introduced by Vivitar in 1978 and manufactured in Japan, based on Cosina's design. It features a fixed 40mm f/1.7 lens with six elements in four groups, notable for its fast maximum aperture and optical sharpness. The camera operates in shutter-priority automatic mode, with shutter speeds from 1/8 to 1/500 second plus Bulb, set via a leaf shutter. Exposure is measured through a CdS cell above the lens, supporting an exposure value (EV) range of 4.5 to 17, and film speeds from ISO 25 to 800. Focusing is manual, utilizing a superimposed rectangle rangefinder patch, and film is advanced with a single-stroke lever. The 35ES also includes a built-in X-sync for flash at all speeds, a 10-second mechanical self-timer, and operates on a 1.35V mercury battery (PX 675).

The Vivitar V3800N is a manual-focus 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera using the Pentax K mount, first introduced by Vivitar in 2001 and remaining available in various markets into at least 2017. Manufactured by Phenix and also marketed as the Phenix DC303N, the camera offers several advanced manual features, including multiple-exposure and depth-of-field preview buttons, as well as a PC connector for off-camera flash capability. It features a vertical-travel, electronic metal focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/2000 second to 1 second plus Bulb mode, and a flash X-sync speed of 1/125 second accessible via both hot shoe and PC socket. The TTL, center-weighted light metering is based on an SPD cell, with ISO range from 25 to 3200. The camera uses a pentaprism viewfinder (0.91x magnification) with LED exposure indicators and a horizontal split-image focusing screen with micro-prism collar. It is powered by two 1.55V LR44 or SR44 batteries, and was available in two color variants: all black, or black with a grey top plate; similar designs were also sold as the Promaster 2500PK Super and Hikari 2002.

The Vivitar XV-5 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced in 1981, notable for its use of the K mount lens system. It was manufactured by Chinon, as indicated by the unique design features like the 3-LED light meter position and self-timer lever, differentiating it from most other Vivitar SLRs, typically made by Cosina. The XV-5 offers a flash sync speed of 1/60 second and a maximum shutter speed of 1/1000 second. Its exposure meter, powered by two LR44 or SR44 batteries, displays over/correct/under exposure via LEDs located just outside the viewfinder eyepiece, within the user's peripheral vision. The camera typically came supplied with a 50mm f/1.9 lens bearing Chinon's distinctive aperture markings. A closely related model, the Vivitar XV-11, shares nearly all specifications, with the primary visual difference being the shape of its self-timer lever.

The Vivitar XC-3 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera featuring an M42 screw lens mount and manufactured by Cosina for Vivitar. Based on the Cosina CSM, it offers TTL (through-the-lens) center-weighted metering, with an LED display in the viewfinder to indicate exposure status. The camera uses an electronically controlled, horizontal-travel focal plane shutter with speeds from 1/1000 to 4 seconds, a mechanical backup at 1/50 sec, and a Bulb mode for long exposures. Metering is activated by a half-press of the shutter, which also stops down the lens, while an electronic self-timer provides a 10-second delay with a blinking LED countdown. The XC-3 requires two 1.5V silver-oxide batteries for most electronic functions; without batteries, only the mechanical shutter speed (M, 1/50 sec) is available. It is compatible with the Vivitar XC-A external automatic exposure unit, allowing aperture priority operation, and includes a flash hot shoe and X-sync PC connector.

The Voigtländer Bessa 66 is a compact folding medium format film camera produced in Germany from 1938 to 1940, and again from 1948 to 1950. It uses 120 rollfilm to produce twelve 6×6 cm exposures per roll, setting it apart from earlier Bessa models, which typically produced 6x9 cm images. Multiple lenses and shutters were used throughout production, including the Voigtar 75mm f/3.5 and Vaskar 75mm f/4.5 pre-war and post-war, as well as the Skopar and Color-Skopar 75mm f/3.5, and Color Heliar 75mm f/3.5. The Bessa 66 was offered in two main versions: a Deluxe model with an optical viewfinder, film counter, and double-exposure prevention, and a simpler Standard model featuring an Albada or frame viewfinder. A distinctive feature of prewar models was a built-in yellow Moment filter that could be swung in or out of the lens path, and all versions employed zone focusing with aligned triangle (3.3m) and circle (10m) marks on the focusing scale. The Bessa 66 is noted for its pocketable form factor and practical features, including a rotating foot that both locks the camera and stabilizes it for tabletop use.

The Voigtländer Bessa L is a compact and lightweight 35mm film camera that was produced by Voigtländer from 1999 to 2002. It features a fully manual operation, allowing photographers to have full control over their exposure settings. The camera has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, making it easy to capture well-exposed images. The Bessa L has a bright and clear viewfinder, which aids in composing and focusing the shot. It has a fixed lens with a focal length of 50mm, which is a versatile option for various types of photography. The camera has a sturdy build quality, with a metal body that ensures durability and longevity. It has a simple and intuitive design, making it suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers. The Bessa L is a reliable and capable camera that delivers excellent image quality and is a great choice for those who prefer manual control and a compact form factor.

The Voigtländer Bessa R2 is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced in 2002. It is a manual focus camera that offers a range of advanced features for photographers. The camera features a bright and clear viewfinder with a built-in rangefinder for precise focusing. It has a sturdy and compact design, making it a great choice for street photography and travel. The Bessa R2 has a top shutter speed of 1/2000s and offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1s to 1/2000s, allowing photographers to capture fast-moving subjects or create long exposure effects. The camera also has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. It accepts Leica M-mount lenses, providing photographers with a wide range of lens options. Overall, the Voigtländer Bessa R2 is a reliable and versatile camera that offers excellent image quality and manual control for film enthusiasts.

The Bessa R2A is a 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Cosina. It features a Leica M mount, allowing it to use a wide range of high-quality lenses. The camera has a built-in light meter with center-weighted metering, making it easy to accurately expose your shots. The R2A has a bright and clear viewfinder, making it easy to focus and compose your images. The Voigtlander Perkeo II is a medium format folding camera produced by Voigtlander in Germany, first introduced in 1952. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera features a coupled rangefinder and is typically equipped with a Color-Skopar 80mm f/3.5 lens, though some versions may have a Vaskar lens. The Perkeo II is fitted with a Synchro-Compur shutter offering speeds from 1 to 1/500 second plus Bulb mode. Film advance is managed by a lever wind mechanism with an automatic frame counter and double exposure prevention. Its compact, folding design makes it a notable example of postwar German engineering in portable medium format cameras.

The Voigtländer Vitessa is a compact and stylish 35mm rangefinder camera that was produced by the German manufacturer Voigtländer in the 1950s. The Wista 45 series consists of metal-bodied, folding-bed technical cameras designed for 4x5-inch large format photography and manufactured in Japan since 1972. They feature double extension bellows that allow for a wide range of camera movements and accommodate lenses from 65 mm to 300 mm with the standard bellows. The modular design supports various accessories, such as extension beds, interchangeable bellows, and an optional 5x7-inch back. There are three main models: the 45VX (base model with geared front rise and multiple movement options), the 45SP (similar to the VX but with an additional geared micro-swing on the rear standard), and the 45RF (features a coupled rangefinder, Albada viewfinder, and lens coupling cams for select focal lengths). All models have a revolving back, use Linhof-type lens panels and international film holders, and include a mechanism to stop down the lens when a film holder is inserted. Each camera weighs approximately 3 kg and is finished in black.

The Yashica 635 is a twin-lens reflex camera introduced by Yashica in 1958 and produced until the early 1970s as a significant export model. This double-format TLR is uniquely capable of shooting both 6x6cm images on 120 film (providing twelve frames per roll) and 35mm photographs using an adapter kit, earning its 635 designation from these dual format capabilities. The camera features a Yashikor 1:3.5 f=80mm lens with a Copal MXV shutter offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second and aperture settings from f/3.5 to f/22. Like most TLR cameras, it operates with waist-level viewing through a focusing screen with an optional magnifying glass for precise focus, and includes a sports finder for alternative composition. The camera lacks an integral light meter, requiring external metering or estimation techniques for proper exposure. Early 1958 models can be identified by the oval Yashica branding between the lenses, which was later changed to bold block letters in subsequent production runs.

The Yashica Electro 35 is a popular rangefinder camera manufactured by Yashica from the 1960s to the 1970s. It features a fixed lens, a built-in light meter, and aperture-priority automatic exposure. It offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1/500 to 30 seconds, allowing for versatile shooting in various lighting conditions. With its classic design and advanced features, the Yashica Electro 35 remains a popular choice among film photography enthusiasts.

The Yashica EM is a twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera manufactured by Yashica and introduced in 1964. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. It includes a built-in selenium cell light meter for uncoupled exposure measurement. The Yashica EM is equipped with a waist-level viewfinder and automatic film counter. Notable for its reliable build and integrated meter, it is part of Yashica's well-regarded TLR lineup.

The Yashica FX-3 is a 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Yashica in 1979. It is compatible with a wide range of Yashica and Contax lenses, allowing for versatile shooting options. Overall, the Yashica FX-3 is a reliable and affordable SLR camera that delivers high-quality results.

The Yashica FX-3 Super 2000 is a 35mm manual-focus single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera released in 1986 and produced until 2002. Manufactured by Cosina, it features a vertical metal-bladed focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 second to 1/2000 second, and has a built-in, battery-powered light meter with a three-LED viewfinder display. The camera body weighs approximately 450 grams (one pound) and is compatible with all manual-focus Yashica/Contax bayonet-mount lenses, including the renowned Carl Zeiss T* lenses. The FX-3 Super 2000 improved upon earlier FX-3 models by including a handgrip, a flash-ready indicator in the viewfinder, a relocated meter switch integrated with the shutter release, a wider ISO range from 25-3200, and a faster maximum shutter speed. Metering operation requires two LR44 (or equivalent 1.5V) batteries, but otherwise, the camera is fully mechanical and can operate without batteries if the meter is not needed. Due to its extended production run, the camera is widely available and remains a popular option for both collectors and those learning manual film photography.

The Yashica Mat-124G is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that was produced by Yashica from 1970 to 1986. The Ikoflex Ic (model 886/16) was a German twin-lens reflex camera manufactured by Zeiss Ikon from 1956 onwards, representing an evolution of the popular Ikoflex series. The camera was available with two lens configurations: either a coated Novar 3.5/75mm or the premium coated Tessar 3.5/75mm lens, both mounted in Prontor-SVS shutters, paired with a Teronar-Anastigmat f/3.5 viewing lens. Notable features included double-exposure prevention, blank frame prevention, M and X flash synchronization, a built-in self-timer, and a sports finder in the hood for quick action photography. The uncoupled light meter provided readings from LV 2 to 16, while an exposure value calculator on the focus knob accommodated film speeds from 5 to 320 ASA. Weighing approximately 1070 grams, the Ikoflex Ic offered advanced metering capabilities while maintaining the classic 6×6 format TLR design that made these cameras popular among both amateur and professional photographers.

The Zeiss Ikon Ikoflex IIa is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera produced by Zeiss Ikon in Germany, introduced around 1952. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The Zenit 12 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera produced by KMZ in Russia from 1983 to 1994. The Zorki 4 is a popular 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Zorki in 1956. It is a fully manual camera, and does not have a lightmeter. As with other Soviet-era rangefinders, the shutter speed selector rotates when the shutter is released, and should not be changed until after the shutter has been cocked.
